memoryText: The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Deuteronomy 29:29 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Deuteronomy 29:29 is a verse about the limits of knowledge and the shape of obedience. It comes at the end of a chapter of warning, and it sets out a balance that every believer needs.

“The secret things belong to the LORD our God.” There are things we do not know and cannot know. Why a particular event happened, how God’s sovereignty and human responsibility work together, what is hidden in the future. These belong to God. This is not a rebuke. It is a relief. We are not required to carry the weight of knowing everything.

“But the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever.” God has spoken. He has made known his character, his promises, and his commands. These are not for specialists alone, but for us and our children. The word “forever” means that the revealed things are a permanent possession. Scripture is a gift to every generation.

“That we may do all the words of this law.” The purpose of revelation is obedience. God does not give us his word only to satisfy curiosity. He gives it so that we may live by it. The practical question is never “What does God know?” but “What has God told me to do?”

For the Christian, the verse is an invitation to humility and to action. Some questions will not be answered in this life. But the gospel has been revealed in Christ, and what we need for life and godliness has been given (2 Peter 1:3). Stop worrying about the secret things. Do what is revealed.
weekInReview: This week you finished the book of Deuteronomy. You read the long section of laws about justice, warfare, and daily life, and the ritual of the firstfruits with its creed. You read the covenant ceremony at Ebal and Gerizim, and the detailed curses of disobedience. You read Moses’ call to choose life and the promise that God would circumcise the heart. In the Psalms, you prayed through the first sections of Psalm 119, which praises the word of God as a source of purity and comfort. You read the Song of Moses, with its image of God as the Rock and the eagle, and then Moses’ last blessing and his death on Mount Nebo. The week taught that God’s word is near, that the heart needs his help to love it, and that even in judgment, he leaves a way back.
reflectionQuestions: Moses said, “The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” What practical difference does it make to you that God’s word is near, and not far off?
The book of Deuteronomy ends with the statement that no prophet had arisen like Moses. How does the New Testament answer that longing, and why does it matter?
Psalm 119 is a long prayer of love for God’s word. How would you describe your own feelings about Scripture, and what would help you to love it more?
prayerPrompts: Give God the things you do not understand and ask him for trust.
Tell him what you want to obey that he has shown you.
